naming-konecta-brand-story.title: Why We Named the Brand Konecta: Comparing the Candidates
naming-konecta-brand-story.summary: How we landed on Konecta after starting with the working name Noriter Beauty Center — the criteria we used to compare candidates and the meaning built into the name.
naming-konecta-brand-story.content:
Before I settled on the name Konecta, I already had another name — one I'd even set up an Instagram account for: Noriter Beauty Center, with the handle @noriter_beautycenter. But I never actually launched the business under that name.

The reason was simple. When I said the word “Noriter” to a Spanish or English speaker for the first time, it sounded unfamiliar and didn't convey any meaning at all. If a brand name can't explain what the business actually does, you've already lost half the battle before you even get to make your pitch.

In the end, the name is the first sentence that shows what kind of bridge this brand is building.

So I went back through the candidate names and narrowed my criteria to three. First, is it easy to pronounce for both Spanish and English speakers? Second, are the Instagram handle and domain actually available to use? Third, does the name itself explain what the business does — connecting Korean cosmetics with the Latin American market? Surprisingly few names satisfied all three at once.

After comparing several candidates, the name I landed on was Konecta — a blend of “Korea” and the Spanish word conecta (“connects”). It's easy to pronounce in both language worlds, and best of all, the meaning of “connection” is built right into the name itself.

Starting from the fact that each of the Andes' different climates comes with different skin concerns, and connecting Latin American consumers with products that actually match their real concerns — instead of just bringing over whatever sells well in Korea — that's the core of what Konecta is trying to do. That's ultimately why I spent so long agonizing over a single name: I believed the name itself had to show what kind of bridge this brand would build.

peru-startup-look-beyond-latin-america.title: Planning to enter the Latin American market? Don't just look at Peru — look at the whole continent
peru-startup-look-beyond-latin-america.summary: Why, when you're building a one-person import business out of Peru, Lima should be your gateway to sizing up the whole South American market — not the end point.
peru-startup-look-beyond-latin-america.content:
Are you preparing to enter Latin America with only the Peruvian market in mind? There's something that people taking their first steps into Peru as solo traders often miss. Peru is definitely a good starting point, but seen against the whole of Latin America, it's just one market among many.

Lima is both the capital of Peru and a city that solo traders preparing to enter Latin America pass through often. That's because it has good logistics access with a port and airport close together, and it also acts as a gateway to other South American countries. So starting your business in Peru naturally gives you the chance to get a feel for the flow of the whole Latin American market at the same time.

In the end, the key to starting a business in Peru is not stopping at Peru alone.

Even within Latin America, consumer tendencies and distribution structures differ from country to country. That means an approach proven in Peru might not work the same way in Chile or Colombia. So rather than preparing several countries at once from the very start, I'd recommend first confirming the response with small-batch trades in Peru, then expanding one by one into other Latin American markets.

Looking at real cases of solo traders who started in Lima and expanded across Latin America, none of them stayed locked into just one country from the beginning. They carried forward the startup experience they built in Peru along with research on neighboring markets, and put that experience to direct use when moving into the next market.

In the end, the key to starting a business in Peru is not stopping at Peru alone. I believe that using Lima as a gateway and picturing all of Latin America on a wider map is the safest approach for anyone jumping into their first market as a solo trader.

solo-trade-latin-america-small-batch.title: Entering the Latin American market as a solo trader: start small
solo-trade-latin-america-small-batch.summary: How to lower your risk by starting with small-batch orders — and how to line up sourcing, customs, and forwarders — when you're taking on markets like Peru or Chile solo.
solo-trade-latin-america-small-batch.content:
If you want to take on a market like Peru or Chile, where Korean cosmetics aren't yet well known, I'd recommend starting with small-batch trades as a solo trader rather than putting in a lot of capital from day one. Solo trading is a way of doing business where an individual can deal directly with overseas buyers without a separate corporation or a large organization, and lately more and more people are using it to take on emerging markets like Latin America.

The most common mistake people make when starting out in trade is setting the order volume too high from the beginning. In a market like Latin America, where consumer response is hard to predict, it's safer to first confirm the response with small-batch trades and then gradually increase the volume. The biggest advantage of small-batch trading is that even if you make a mistake, you still have room to recover.

The practical work you need to prepare in the early stages of a startup can be broken down into three main areas: sourcing, customs, and forwarders. Sourcing is the process of deciding which products to supply and under what terms; customs refers to the documents and procedures needed to clear the local customs authority in Latin America; and a forwarder is the company that actually transports the cargo. Since sanitary registration and customs standards differ from country to country in Latin America, it's safer to check them in advance for each country you plan to enter.

Peru and Chile also differ in consumer tendencies and distribution structure, so it's hard to apply experience from one country directly to the other. You also need to account for the possibility that shipping times may run longer than expected — and the surest way to get a feel for these variables is to run into them directly through small-batch trades.

To sum up, the key to entering the Latin American market as a solo trader is lowering your risk with small-batch trades while learning the sourcing, customs, and forwarder processes one at a time. Rather than waiting until you're perfectly prepared to start, starting small and building up experience is the safer approach in a market with as many variables as Latin America.
